structure.rationale: The book explains one real application, sunprema/file_cleaner, to a reader who knows only basic Rust. The order follows the program's own data flow rather than a language syllabus: what the tool does and how the crate is laid out, then the one mechanism everything else exists to serve (the APFS clone and the clonefile FFI call), then the domain types, then the pipeline that produces candidates — walk, index, funnel — then the two pieces of Rust craft that make the second half readable (the error split, and the ApfsAdapter trait seam), and finally the conservative replacement engine in the order it actually runs: preflight, the journaled transaction, metadata fidelity, and crash recovery. Each chapter teaches a Rust idea where the code forces it to appear — ownership in the walker, borrow discipline in the index, closures and rayon in the funnel, trait objects at the platform boundary, enums as state machines in the journal — so no concept is introduced before the program needs it.
structure.audience: A developer who knows the basics of Rust (syntax, structs, Result, the borrow checker as a concept) and wants to read a real, non-trivial systems application end to end.

claims.text: filecleaner is a duplicate-file space reclaimer for macOS/APFS: it finds files with byte-identical content and, instead of deleting anything, replaces each duplicate with an APFS clone of a chosen source file.
Every reclaimed file keeps its path, its metadata and its independence; the data blocks are shared on disk copy-on-write until a file is modified.
The project ships as a CLI binary named `filecleaner` and a library crate named `file_cleaner`; a native SwiftUI app under FileCleanerApp/ drives the same engine.
Cargo.toml declares edition 2024 and version 0.1.0, with an explicit [[bin]] (name filecleaner, path src/main.rs) and [lib] (name file_cleaner, path src/lib.rs).
The runtime dependencies are anyhow, blake3, clap (derive), libc, rand, rayon, rusqlite (bundled), serde (derive), serde_json, sha2, thiserror and walkdir; tempfile is a dev-dependency.
The four CLI subcommands are scan, scans, groups and reclaim; --db and --json are global flags.
`filecleaner reclaim --group <id>` is a dry run by default — the destructive path requires --confirm.
src/lib.rs exposes six engine entry points: run_scan, run_funnel, list_groups, dry_run_group, reclaim_group and recover (plus list_scans and get_group).
The module tree separates concerns by layer: scanner (traversal), index (persistence + hashing), model/policy (domain), txn (the transaction engine) and apfs (all unsafe, Darwin-specific code).
The index database lives at ~/.filecleaner/index.db by default, overridable with --db.
main() calls recover(&db_path) before dispatching any subcommand, so an interrupted transaction is repaired on every launch.

pitfalls: Reading the module tree as layers of abstraction rather than a blast radius: `apfs/` is not merely 'the platform layer', it is the only place `unsafe` is allowed to appear.
Assuming `reclaim` without a flag is destructive — the dry run is the default, and `--dry-run` exists only to say so explicitly.

claims.text: clonefile() asks APFS to create a new inode that shares the source file's data extents; no bytes are copied up front.
The cloned file shares its data blocks with the source but has its own copy of attributes and extended attributes, initially identical to the source's.
Later writes to either file are private to that file: only modified blocks get their own physical storage (copy-on-write divergence).
The destination must not exist; clonefile fails with EEXIST if it does.
clonefile fails with EXDEV when source and destination are not on the same filesystem — cloning is a same-volume feature.

A clone has its own inode and its own metadata, unlike a hard link which is the same inode under another name; editing one clone does not change the other, whereas editing through one hard link changes 'the file' seen through all of them.
Finder and du report each clone at full logical size even though only a fraction of the data is physically stored; the volume's free space is what actually improves.
file_cleaner's clone_file wrapper converts both paths to CStrings, calls libc::clonefile inside an unsafe block, and maps a non-zero return to io::Error::last_os_error().

The wrapper passes CLONE_NOFOLLOW (0x0001), a constant it declares itself because the libc crate does not bind it — the code comment says so explicitly: 'From <sys/clonefile.h>; not bound by the libc crate.'
The transaction engine relies on the EEXIST behaviour: it never clones onto a live target, only onto a fresh temp path.
On non-macOS targets clone_file is compiled to a stub returning io::ErrorKind::Unsupported, so the crate still builds and tests elsewhere.
An integration test proves the clone is a real clone and not a hard link: the cloned file has a different inode from the source, and writing to the clone leaves the source's contents unchanged.
Another integration test asserts clone_file returns raw OS error EEXIST when the destination already exists, and leaves that destination's contents untouched.

APFS clone support is not universal: the man page notes a volume can be tested for clonefile() support via getattrlist(2)'s ATTR_VOL_CAPABILITIES / VOL_CAP_INT_CLONE. file_cleaner instead checks the filesystem type name via statfs and requires it to be exactly "apfs".

tests/apfs_integration.rs, verbatim — the test that pins down what a clone is

pitfalls: Expecting `du` or Finder's size column to drop after reclaiming: they report logical size per file. Only the volume's free space reflects shared extents.

Treating a clone as redundancy. Both copies point at the same physical blocks on the same volume; if those blocks are lost, every clone is lost with them (README's explicit 'not a backup tool' warning).

Forgetting that `unsafe` here is about the FFI boundary, not about danger in the abstract: the pointers passed to clonefile must stay alive for the duration of the call, which is why the CStrings are bound to locals first.

claims.text: model.rs defines VolumeId(pub u64) and ContentId(pub [u8; 32]) as tuple-struct newtypes over primitives, so a device id can never be silently used where a content hash is expected.

FileEntry records path, dev, ino, nlink, size, mtime_sec, mtime_nsec and rsrc_len — the resource-fork length, which is part of the grouping key because files whose forks differ are not macOS-identical even when their data forks match.

DuplicateGroup holds id, dev, size, rsrc_len, sha256 and a Vec<GroupMember>; the doc comment states that byte comparison still happens at reclaim time and that this grouping only nominates candidates.
DuplicateGroup::source() finds the member with is_source set and panics with 'every group has a source' if none exists — an invariant the database layer guarantees by storing source_file_id NOT NULL.

eligible_targets() returns an iterator over members whose inode differs from the source's and whose nlink == 1: hardlinks of the source already share storage, and replacing one path of a multi-link inode would silently break the link relationship for paths outside our view.
logical_duplicate_bytes() is size × (distinct inodes − 1); estimated_reclaimable_bytes() is size × eligible target count. The two differ precisely by the members that are excluded for safety.
ScanStats is a plain counter struct deriving Debug, Default, Clone, PartialEq, Eq and serde::Serialize, so the same value prints for humans and serializes to JSON for the GUI.
The default source policy is deterministic: oldest modification time wins, ties broken by lexicographically smallest path, so repeated runs pick the same source.
choose_source compares tuples (mtime_sec, mtime_nsec, &path), relying on Rust's lexicographic tuple ordering to express the whole policy in one comparison.
The source is only ever read, never written, during a reclamation transaction — stated in policy.rs's doc comment and enforced by the executor.
eligible_targets uses `filter(move |m| ...)` so the closure takes ownership of the captured source_ino, letting the returned iterator outlive the local binding.

snippets.note: src/model.rs, verbatim — the three methods that encode the safety policy

pitfalls: Confusing 'logical duplicates' with 'reclaimable': hardlinked members are counted in the first and deliberately excluded from the second.
Assuming two files with the same data fork are the same file on macOS — a differing resource fork makes them different, which is why rsrc_len is in the group key.
Reaching for `.filter(|m| ...)` without `move` and then being surprised the iterator cannot be returned: the closure would borrow the local `source_ino`.

claims.text: walk_roots builds a WalkDir iterator per root with follow_links(false), so symlinks are never followed.

Package directories are pruned with WalkDir::filter_entry, which skips a directory and its whole subtree — but only at depth > 0, so a package passed explicitly as a scan root counts as the user choosing to traverse it.
Because filter_entry takes an Fn closure that cannot mutate its environment, the package counter is a Cell<u64> and is incremented through interior mutability, then folded into stats after the walk.

Each entry is classified in order: directories, symlinks, other non-regular files, the tool's own .filecleaner.* artifacts, unreadable metadata, zero-byte files — and only what survives becomes a FileEntry.
Overlapping roots are deduplicated with a HashSet of paths, so scanning both ~/a and ~/a/b indexes each file once.
Files with nlink > 1 are counted in stats.hardlinked but are still recorded; the exclusion happens later, at grouping and preflight time.
entry.into_path() consumes the DirEntry to hand its PathBuf to the FileEntry without cloning the path — an ownership move rather than a copy.
Unix metadata (dev, ino, nlink, mtime_nsec) is only visible after `use std::os::unix::fs::MetadataExt`, an extension trait that adds platform methods to std::fs::Metadata.
Resource-fork length is read at scan time via forks::resource_fork_len, which calls getxattr with a null buffer to ask only for the size, and returns 0 on any failure.

filter.rs lists 21 macOS package extensions (app, appex, band, bundle, docset, fcpbundle, framework, imovielibrary, kext, lproj, mpkg, photoslibrary, pkg, playground, plugin, prefpane, qlgenerator, scptd, tvlibrary, xcodeproj, xcworkspace, xpc) and matches them case-insensitively.
OWN_ARTIFACT_PREFIX is ".filecleaner." — temp and backup files created by the tool's own transactions, which must never be scanned as duplicate candidates.
The walker never propagates an error: an unreadable entry increments stats.errors and the walk continues, so one permission-denied folder cannot abort a scan.

snippets.note: src/apfs/forks.rs, verbatim — note the c"…" C-string literal and the let-else
src/scanner/walker.rs unit test, abridged (assertions on file names elided)

pitfalls: Using a plain `let mut n = 0` counter inside filter_entry — it will not compile, because filter_entry needs an `Fn`, not an `FnMut`.
Assuming `follow_links(false)` means symlinks are ignored: they still show up as entries, they are just not traversed. The walker counts and skips them explicitly.
Expecting `entry.metadata()` to follow the symlink — with follow_links(false) walkdir returns the link's own metadata.

claims.text: The index is a SQLite database opened through rusqlite with the bundled feature, so SQLite is compiled into the binary and there is no system dependency.
Db::open sets journal_mode = WAL, synchronous = NORMAL and foreign_keys = ON, then runs the schema and a migration pass.
WAL mode is chosen so the transaction journal can rely on durable state transitions and so a review UI can read while a scan runs.
There are four tables: scans, files, groups and txn_journal, plus four indexes.
files carries the scan's raw observation (path, dev, ino, nlink, size, mtime, rsrc_len) and three columns the funnel fills in later: fingerprint, sha256 and group_id, all nullable.
A UNIQUE (scan_id, path) constraint plus INSERT OR IGNORE makes re-inserting the same file during a scan a no-op instead of an error.
txn_journal deliberately has no foreign keys, because journal rows must outlive group rebuilds and scans so recovery always has what it needs.
Db owns its Connection; methods that only read take &self while methods that write take &mut self, so the borrow checker enforces at compile time that no read is in flight during a write.
Bulk writes go through conn.transaction() with a prepared statement reused in a loop, and the statement is dropped in an inner scope before tx.commit() so the borrow ends.
rusqlite's query_map returns an iterator of Result rows, so every read loop in db.rs pushes `row?` into a Vec — the error of a single row propagates rather than being silently skipped.
latest_scan_id maps QueryReturnedNoRows to Ok(None) and leaves every other error an Err, converting 'nothing found' from an error into a value.
migrate() reads PRAGMA table_info(files) and adds rsrc_len and group_id columns if missing, because CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS never adds columns to an existing table.
rebuild_groups clears files.group_id before deleting rows from groups, so the files → groups foreign key never dangles.
journal_set_state reads the current state, parses it, and refuses an illegal transition with an error — the state machine is enforced at the database layer, not only in the executor.
Db::open uses a Rust 2024 let-chain (`if let Some(parent) = path.parent() && !parent.as_os_str().is_empty()`), a feature stabilized in Rust 1.88 and available only in the 2024 edition.

src/index/db.rs, verbatim — 'not found' turned from an error into a value

pitfalls: Forgetting the inner scope around a prepared statement: `tx.commit()` moves the transaction, and the statement borrows it, so it must be dropped first.
Treating `query_map` results as infallible — each row is a Result, and swallowing it hides a corrupt row as a missing one.
Assuming `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` upgrades a schema. It does not touch an existing table; new columns need an explicit migration.

claims.text: The funnel has three narrowing stages before grouping: (dev, size, rsrc_len) buckets, a partial BLAKE3 fingerprint, then a full streaming SHA-256.

Stage one is pure SQL and reads no file contents: a bucket qualifies only if it contains at least two distinct inodes (HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT ino) >= 2), which both eliminates singletons and collapses hardlinks to one entity.
Stage two hashes only the first, middle and last 64 KiB (RANGE_LEN = 64 * 1024); files of 3 × RANGE_LEN or smaller — 192 KiB — are hashed whole because the ranges would overlap.
The fingerprint uses BLAKE3 for speed, while the stored content identity is SHA-256; the code comments call the fingerprint 'cheap' and the SHA-256 the 'stored identity'.
Stage three streams the whole data fork through SHA-256 in 1 MiB chunks.
Every hashing read is preceded by verify_unchanged, which re-stats the file and returns HashError::Stale unless it is still a regular file with the same size and the same mtime to the nanosecond.
A stale candidate is not an error: the funnel counts it in report.stale and it simply drops out of the funnel.
Both hash stages share one generic helper, hash_stage, parameterized by a closure `impl Fn(&HashCandidate) -> Result<[u8; 32], HashError> + Sync`.
Parallelism comes from rayon's par_iter over the candidate slice; the results are collected first and only then folded into the mutable report, so no lock is needed.
Results persist after each stage (set_fingerprints, set_sha256s), and the candidate queries only select rows whose column IS NULL — so a re-run resumes instead of rehashing.
rebuild_groups groups by (dev, size, rsrc_len, sha256) with at least two distinct inodes, picks a source with policy::choose_source, and writes one groups row plus a group_id on every member.

Hashes only nominate candidates. The final authority is a byte-for-byte comparison of both the data fork and the resource fork, performed inside the transaction — stated in README.md, in model.rs's doc comments, and implemented in executor.rs.
A funnel integration test constructs same-size files differing only in a middle byte, proving the fingerprint splits them without a full read.

src/index/funnel.rs, verbatim — one generic stage, parallel then sequential
src/index/funnel.rs, verbatim — the whole funnel in one function

pitfalls: Believing SHA-256 equality licenses a destructive replacement. The code does not: it re-reads both files byte for byte inside the transaction.
Sampling first/middle/last on small files: the ranges overlap and the sample degenerates, which is why files ≤192 KiB are hashed whole.
Mutating a shared counter from inside par_iter. The code sidesteps it entirely by collecting first and folding afterwards.

claims.text: file_cleaner uses both error crates, split by purpose: anyhow::Result at the engine and CLI edges, thiserror-derived enums wherever a caller must branch on the failure.
The ecosystem convention is exactly this split — thiserror for libraries whose callers need to match on specific cases, anyhow for application code where the error is logged or displayed.
There are three thiserror enums: HashError (2 variants), PreflightError (11 variants) and TxnError (6 variants).
HashError::Stale exists so the funnel can distinguish 'the file changed' from 'the read failed' and count them separately.
`#[from] std::io::Error` generates the From impl that makes `?` convert an io::Error into the enum automatically.
`#[error(transparent)]` forwards Display and source to the wrapped error, so an io failure reads as itself rather than gaining a redundant prefix.

PreflightError's variants are the safety policy written as a type: TargetNotRegular, SourceNotRegular, TargetChanged, TargetHardlinked, SameInode, DifferentVolume, NotApfs, TargetImmutable, SourceUnreadable, DirNotWritable and Io.
Each variant's #[error("…")] string is the message the user actually sees in the CLI's SKIP line, so the error type and the user-facing copy are the same text.

TxnError::Preflight uses `#[from] PreflightError`, which is what lets execute() start with `planner::preflight(plan, adapter)?` and have a preflight failure become a transaction failure with no glue code.
anyhow::Context is used to attach human context to io failures — 'cannot access scan root {}' in run_scan, 'cannot open database {}' in Db::open.
lib.rs also uses .context() on an Option to turn None into an actionable error: 'no completed scans in the index; run `filecleaner scan` first'.
Two public type aliases keep the engine's signatures readable: DryRunResult = (TxnPlan, Result<(), PreflightError>) and ReclaimResult = (TxnPlan, Result<TxnReport, TxnError>).
Because main returns anyhow::Result<()>, a `?` anywhere in main prints the error chain and exits non-zero with no explicit handling.

#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
pub enum PreflightError {
    #[error("target is not a regular file")]
    TargetNotRegular,
    #[error("source is not a regular file")]
    SourceNotRegular,
    #[error("target changed since scan (size, mtime, or inode differs)")]
    TargetChanged,
    #[error("target has additional hardlinks; replacing it would break them")]
    TargetHardlinked,
    #[error("source and target are the same inode")]
    SameInode,
    #[error("source and target are on different volumes; APFS clones are same-volume only")]
    DifferentVolume,
    #[error("target volume is not APFS")]
    NotApfs,
    #[error("target is immutable (uchg/schg flag set)")]
    TargetImmutable,
    #[error("source is not readable: {0}")]
    SourceUnreadable(String),
    #[error("target directory is not writable")]
    DirNotWritable,
    #[error(transparent)]
    Io(#[from] std::io::Error),
}

}

src/lib.rs, verbatim — Context on an Option turns None into an actionable message

pitfalls: Reaching for anyhow inside the library core: the caller then cannot tell 'target changed' from 'disk full', and the CLI could not print a specific SKIP reason.
Writing #[error("io error: {0}")] where #[error(transparent)] is meant — the message gains a prefix that duplicates what the inner error already says.
Assuming `?` converts between arbitrary error types. It calls From, which is exactly what #[from] generates for you.

claims.text: src/apfs/mod.rs opens with a module doc comment stating that all Darwin-specific and unsafe code lives in this module, and that everything above it stays platform-neutral and depends on the ApfsAdapter trait so tests can inject failures at any step without touching a real filesystem.
ApfsAdapter has seven methods: clone_file, device_of, is_apfs, snapshot_metadata, restore_metadata, read_resource_fork and bsd_flags.
The trait requires Send + Sync, so an implementation can be shared across threads.
RealApfs is a unit struct with no fields — the production implementation is pure delegation to the free functions in clone.rs, volume.rs, metadata.rs and forks.rs.
bsd_flags is the one method with a cfg split inside the impl: on macOS it reads st_flags via std::os::macos::fs::MetadataExt, elsewhere it returns Ok(0).
The transaction engine takes `&dyn ApfsAdapter` — dynamic dispatch through a trait object — so one compiled executor works with both the real adapter and any test double.
tests/fault_injection.rs defines a FaultyAdapter that wraps RealApfs and fails (or mutates the target) at a chosen step, driven by a Fault enum with six variants.

The fork-read fault uses an AtomicU32 call counter because the trait methods take &self, not &mut self: the executor calls read_resource_fork three times — source, target, temp — and the fault fires on the third.

Every fault case asserts the same invariant: the target still has the expected content, keeps its original inode, no .filecleaner.* artifacts remain, the source is untouched, and the journal row is terminal 'rolled-back' with a recorded cause.

Two of the six faults are not failures at all: MutateEarly and MutateLate rewrite the target mid-transaction to prove the byte compare and the post-rename stat check each catch a user edit in their own window.

planner.rs's own unit tests use a different double, FakeVolumes, whose volume answers are scripted while everything else is real; its unreachable!() bodies document what preflight must never do — 'preflight never clones', 'preflight never snapshots'.

snippets.note: tests/fault_injection.rs, verbatim — &self forces an atomic counter
tests/fault_injection.rs, verbatim — one assertion function, six faults

pitfalls: Designing the trait around 'the filesystem' in general. This one is deliberately narrow: exactly the seven operations a reclamation needs, which is what makes a complete test double a hundred lines rather than a thousand.
Expecting `&mut self` on trait methods so a test double can count calls — the shared-reference signature is what forces (and rewards) an atomic counter.

claims.text: make_plan builds a TxnPlan per target: source and target paths, a temp path and a backup path both in the target's own directory, the size, and an ExpectedTarget snapshot of ino/size/mtime.
Temp and backup names share one random 16-hex-digit token from rand::random::<u64>(), formatted as .filecleaner.<token>.tmp and .filecleaner.<token>.backup.
Both staging paths live in the target's directory so that both renames are same-directory and therefore atomic within that filesystem.
ExpectedTarget carries what the scan recorded, so preflight can re-check the live file against it and never touch a target that changed since scanning.
preflight reads only — it never mutates the filesystem — which is what makes the dry-run path pure.
Content identity is deliberately NOT checked in preflight; the executor byte-compares both forks inside the journaled transaction.

The check order is: target exists and is a regular file → ino/size/mtime match the plan → nlink == 1 → source is a regular file → source and target are not the same inode → same device → volume is APFS → target is not immutable → source opens for reading → target directory is writable.
A missing target is mapped to PreflightError::TargetChanged rather than an Io error, because from the user's point of view a deleted file is a file that changed.
Immutability is tested against UF_IMMUTABLE (0x0000_0002) and SF_IMMUTABLE (0x0002_0000), constants declared in planner.rs.
Directory writability is checked with libc::access(dir, W_OK | X_OK), which is read-only and therefore safe during a dry run.

dry_run_group maps every eligible target to (plan, preflight verdict) and mutates nothing; reclaim_group loops the same targets through executor::execute, each an independent transaction so one failure rolls back that target only.
A test writes to the target after planning and asserts preflight returns TargetChanged; another deletes it and asserts the same variant.
A fault-injection test makes the target's directory mode 0o555 and asserts PreflightError::DirNotWritable.

pitfalls: Treating preflight as sufficient. It is a cheap filter; the expensive, authoritative checks happen inside the transaction, where the window between check and act is closed by the rename.
Using fs::metadata instead of fs::symlink_metadata: the former follows symlinks, and a symlinked target must be rejected, not resolved.
Putting the temp file in /tmp. It would land on a different volume — clonefile would fail with EXDEV, and the final rename would no longer be atomic.

claims.text: The executor's doc comment lists the whole sequence: preflight → journal prepared → snapshot target metadata → byte-compare both forks (final authority) → clone source to temp → restore target metadata onto temp → verify temp → journal backup-created → rename(target, backup) → journal swapped → rename(temp, target) → fsync dir → final validation → remove backup → journal committed.
execute() runs preflight, inserts the journal row, then delegates the mutating half to run(), whose Err carries a Progress value describing how far the filesystem was actually mutated.
Progress is a private four-variant enum: Clean, TempCreated, BackupRenamed, TargetSwapped — the rollback plan is chosen from it, not guessed from the filesystem.
The byte comparison happens inside the transaction, on both the data fork and the resource fork, and is the final authority before any replacement.
data_forks_identical streams both files in 1 MiB buffers, short-circuits on a length mismatch, and uses a read_full helper so a short read is not mistaken for a difference.

The temp clone is verified four ways before it may replace anything: file type and size, permission bits against the snapshot, byte-identical data fork against the source, and identical resource fork.
Each journal state is written before the filesystem step it precedes: BackupCreated before rename(target, backup), Swapped before rename(temp, target).

Immediately after rename(target, backup), the executor re-stats the backup and compares ino/size/mtime against the plan's expectations — rename preserves the inode, so a target mutated at any point since preflight shows up here and rolls back.
The directory is fsync'd after the swap for durability, but best-effort: the result is discarded with `let _ =`.
Final validation re-checks type, size and byte identity at the target path; only after it passes is the backup removed and the journal marked committed.
Once run() returns Ok, the code never rolls back: a failure to delete the backup or to mark the journal committed becomes a warning saying recovery will clean it up.
A failed rollback is not swallowed — the journal's error text becomes '<error>; ROLLBACK INCOMPLETE: <rollback error>'.
The source file is never opened for writing at any point in the transaction.
MetadataSnapshot restore warnings (ownership, ACL, birth time) are carried up into TxnReport.warnings rather than failing the transaction.

An integration test proves the happy path: same content, a NEW inode at the target path, the target's original mode and mtime preserved, the source's inode and bytes unchanged, and a committed journal row.

An adversarial test writes different bytes of the same length and restores the mtime so every stat check passes, then asserts the transaction still fails on identity and the target is untouched — proving stat checks alone would have been wrong.

pitfalls: Cloning straight onto the target path. clonefile refuses (EEXIST) — and even if it did not, there would be a moment with no file at that path.
Journaling a state after doing the filesystem step. The whole recovery argument depends on the record being durable first.
Rolling back after final validation succeeded: the user's file has already been correctly replaced, and 'undoing' it would be the destructive act.

claims.text: clonefile gives the new file its own copy of the SOURCE's attributes and extended attributes — which is exactly why a replacement must reapply the TARGET's metadata afterwards.
metadata.rs's module doc states the goal plainly: the clone starts with the source's metadata, and restoring the snapshot makes it indistinguishable from the target it replaces.

MetadataSnapshot captures mode (st_mode & 0o7777, including setuid/setgid/sticky), uid, gid, BSD flags, atime, mtime, optional birth time, all extended attributes sorted by name, and the ACL in text form.
The xattr list includes com.apple.FinderInfo and com.apple.ResourceFork, so Finder tags, custom icons and resource forks ride along with the ordinary metadata.

Restore order is deliberate and documented: xattrs and ACL first, then ownership (because chown clears setuid bits), then mode, then times (earlier steps touch them), and BSD flags last (an immutable flag would block every other step).
Restore first removes any xattr present on the clone that the target did not have — strays inherited from the source — then writes the target's set.
Hard failures on mode, xattrs and times return Err; ownership, ACL and birth-time restoration degrade to warnings in RestoreOutcome because they can require privileges the process legitimately lacks.
listxattr and getxattr are called twice each — once with a null buffer to learn the size, once to read — and retry on ERANGE, because the attribute list can grow between the two calls.

Darwin's ACL API is not bound by the libc crate, so metadata.rs hand-declares acl_get_link_np, acl_set_link_np, acl_to_text, acl_from_text, acl_init and acl_free in an `unsafe extern "C"` block, with ACL_TYPE_EXTENDED = 0x100.
When the target had no ACL, restore installs an empty ACL (acl_init(0)) rather than doing nothing, so nothing inherited from the source survives.
Birth time is restored through setattrlist, also hand-declared, with a #[repr(C)] AttrList struct, ATTR_CMN_CRTIME = 0x0000_0200 and FSOPT_NOFOLLOW.
get_acl_text has to interpret ENOENT from acl_get_link_np as 'no ACL', not 'no file'.
Every xattr call passes XATTR_NOFOLLOW, and chown is done with lchown, so no operation can be redirected through a symlink.
forks.rs treats ENOATTR from a resource-fork read as an empty fork rather than an error, and resource_forks_equal is a byte comparison of the two reads.

An integration test round-trips a snapshot: mode 0o640, three xattrs including a resource fork and a Finder tag, and a specific mtime — restored onto a stand-in file that carried a stray xattr, which must vanish.

pitfalls: Assuming the clone arrives blank. It arrives wearing the source's clothes — including the source's Finder tags and resource fork — which is why strays must be removed explicitly.
Restoring mode before ownership: chown clears setuid/setgid bits, so the order would silently drop them.
Restoring BSD flags early: an immutable flag would block every subsequent step on the very file you are still configuring.
Sizing an xattr buffer once. Between the size call and the read call, the attribute can grow — hence the ERANGE retry loop.

claims.text: TxnState has five variants: Prepared, BackupCreated, Swapped, Committed, RolledBack; the first three are non-terminal.

The doc comment states the recovery rule per state: Prepared means nothing user-visible has changed (roll back); BackupCreated means the target may have been renamed to the backup (roll back); Swapped means the clone was fully verified (roll forward).

can_transition encodes the legal edges: Prepared→BackupCreated, BackupCreated→Swapped, Swapped→Committed, and any of the three non-terminal states→RolledBack. Nothing else is allowed, and terminal states have no outgoing edges.
Db::journal_set_state refuses an illegal transition with an error rather than performing it, so a bug in the executor fails loudly instead of corrupting the recovery invariants.
journal_incomplete selects rows whose state is 'prepared', 'backup-created' or 'swapped' — precisely the interrupted transactions recovery must repair.
Recovery from Prepared deletes any temp file and marks the row rolled-back with 'interrupted before swap; target untouched'.
Recovery from BackupCreated renames the backup back to the target if and only if the target is missing and the backup exists, then removes any temp, then marks rolled-back.

Recovery from Swapped rolls FORWARD: it completes rename(temp, target) if the target is missing, fsyncs the directory, removes the backup and marks the row committed — safe precisely because the temp clone passed full verification before 'swapped' was journaled.
If the clone was lost mid-crash — no target, but a backup exists — recovery falls back to the original: rename(backup, target), remove temp, mark rolled-back.
If neither target, temp nor backup exists, recovery marks the row rolled-back with 'manual attention required' and reports 'UNRESOLVED'.
recover_all returns a human-readable line per repair, formatted as 'txn #<id> (<target>): <action>', which the CLI prints as 'recovered: …'.

Recovery is idempotent and safe to run on every launch: an empty journal is a no-op, terminal rows are ignored, and lib.rs::recover returns early with no repairs when the database file does not even exist.

Integration tests reconstruct the exact on-disk state a kill would leave at each journal state — prepared, backup-created, swapped, and swapped-with-lost-clone — and assert the resulting repair, plus that a second recovery run finds nothing left to do.
The user-facing consequence, as the user guide puts it: if the Mac loses power mid-reclaim, the next filecleaner command repairs the interrupted transaction automatically and prints what it did.

pitfalls: Rolling back from `swapped`. The clone at that point has already passed every verification; undoing the swap would throw away correct work and reintroduce the duplicate.
Recovering from the filesystem alone. Without the journal, a lone `.filecleaner.*.backup` next to a target is ambiguous — it could be a pre-swap backup or a post-swap leftover.
Making recovery optional. It runs before every subcommand precisely because the user is never asked to clean up by hand.
